idiom_name: assign the attribute first, then super().__init__(self.data)
implementation_notes: Python has no base-before-member initialisation rule to work around: a class's initialisation is simply the code in __init__, so the payload is created first and passed to the base - self.buf = make_buffer(fd) followed by super().__init__(self.buf) - and cooperative super() (the MRO-based call-next-method the tutorial describes) takes care of the rest. What replaces the C++ helper base is statement order inside one method; the classic structure (a base that owns the member so that it is constructed before another base) has no counterpart, because a base is initialised by an explicit call whose position you choose, not by a fixed language rule. The classic form is justified only when the 'base' is genuinely a superclass and the member must exist before its __init__ runs - which in Python is achieved by assigning it first.
pitfalls: The order is a convention of your own code: nothing in the class definition enforces it, so calling super().__init__() first (or letting a cooperative chain reach it early) leaves the attribute unset and any base code reading it raises AttributeError later, far from the mistake.

Cooperative multiple inheritance reorders things behind your back: with super() the next class in the MRO may be a sibling mixin rather than the base you had in mind, so a payload assigned 'before super()' can still be written after the base that consumes it if that base was reached through another path.

Declaring the attribute as a dataclass field or an __slots__ entry changes the picture: the generated __init__ fills the field, so the value must be passed as an argument instead of assigned, and mixing both styles silently produces two attributes.
